subtype: Approach: asking a parent to remind him at night [Action]
passage: In the cricket club's changing room, Coach Reena read the list for tomorrow's match: whites, pads, ID card, water bottle. Hemant nodded, but his stomach dropped. Last month he had forgotten his ID card and been kept out of the warm-up. He knew his own head. In the car park, he told his father, "Papa, tonight after dinner, please ask me what I need for tomorrow. Then I'll pack." Papa smiled. "Whites, pads, ID, water," said Hemant. "Ask me." At nine o'clock Papa asked, Hemant listed all four, and zipped the kitbag shut. He was at the gate with everything at eight the next morning.

qa.q: What four things did the coach list for the match?
qa.a: The coach listed whites, pads, ID card and water bottle.

qa.q: Why did Hemant ask his father to remind him?
qa.a: Hemant remembered forgetting the ID card last month and knew his own head, so he felt worried and wanted a helper for this important list. 😰

qa.q: What alternative approach could Hemant use next time, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could keep a written checklist inside the kitbag or pack right after practice. A list does not depend on anyone else being free.

qa.q: How might Papa see Hemant's request?
qa.a: Papa smiled and asked at nine as agreed, so Papa probably feels glad that Hemant took responsibility and asked for help.

grounding: Knowing he tends to forget, a boy asks his father to quiz him in the evening about what he needs, using another person as a memory helper.

subtype: Approach: taking turns by the clock [Action]
passage: The two brothers, Harsha and Bhavesh, had one tablet between them and a fight every afternoon. "I've been playing for less time!" "No, you've had it for an hour!" Then Harsha had an idea. He fetched the kitchen timer from the shelf, a round white one that ticked. "Thirty minutes each. When it rings, the tablet moves." Bhavesh went first, watching the dial go round. When the bell rang he grumbled and handed it over. Harsha set the timer again. There was no argument about who had played longer, because the clock decided, and by evening their mother found them side by side, waiting for their turns.

qa.q: How long did each brother get with the tablet?
qa.a: Each brother got thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when the fight about time kept happening?
qa.a: Harsha was probably frustrated and tired of arguing, which led him to look for a fairer way with the timer. 😠

qa.q: What alternative approach could the brothers use, and why?
qa.a: They could pick a two-player game they both enjoy, or agree on days for each of them. Either way the fight over minutes would be gone.

qa.q: How might Bhavesh see the timer?
qa.a: Bhavesh grumbled when the bell rang, so Bhavesh probably found it fair but also disappointing to give the tablet up on time.

grounding: Two brothers who share one tablet use a kitchen timer to give each thirty minutes, so the fixed time settles the argument about who played longer.

subtype: Approach: grabbing it first and refusing to hand over [Pitfall]
passage: Note from Thomas, evening. I want to record what happened today so we can talk to both children. Susan got to the sofa first, picked up the remote and, when her younger brother Suraj asked for it, hid it behind a cushion. "I was here first," she said. Suraj shouted and then cried. My wife and I came in to find both of them red-faced and the remote nowhere to be seen. It was no longer about the television, it was about who was in charge. Neither child watched anything, and the evening was spoilt for everyone. Tomorrow we will sit down together.

qa.q: Where did Susan hide the remote?
qa.a: Susan hid the remote behind a cushion.

qa.q: What might Susan have been feeling when she said 'I was here first'?
qa.a: Susan was probably feeling possessive and defensive, wanting to keep what she got to first.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Susan and Suraj try, and why?
qa.a: They could take turns using a timer or agree on a plan for which days each of them picks. A shared plan means no one has to win by hiding the remote.

qa.q: How does the fight look to Suraj?
qa.a: Suraj shouted and cried when the remote was hidden, so Suraj felt shut out and treated unfairly by an older sister.

grounding: An older sister takes the remote and hides it because she got there first, the brother complains, the parents are upset, and sharing becomes a fight over power.

subtype: Approach: agreeing to a plan with days for each [Thinking]
passage: Darshan, let me tell you about my brother Mohan and the television. We were always fighting. One Sunday I said, "Let's stop and think. What is fair?" We looked at the week. "Monday, Wednesday, Friday for me," I said, "and Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday for you." Mohan frowned. "But you have exams on Fridays." I thought about it. "Then I'll take a Saturday instead of a Friday, and you take Friday." We shook on it. Some weeks it did not suit one of us, and we changed a day, but the rule itself never broke. I'm Pooja, and I still remember how fair it felt.

qa.q: Which days did the narrator first ask for?
qa.a: Pooja first asked for Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

qa.q: What did Mohan want when saying that Pooja had exams on Fridays?
qa.a: Mohan wanted the plan to be fair for both, noticing that Fridays would not suit Pooja's studying.

qa.q: What choice in the story kept the plan fair, and why?
qa.a: Swapping a Friday for a Saturday kept it fair, because the days matched each child's homework and both felt heard.

qa.q: How did the plan look from Mohan's side?
qa.a: Mohan got a say in changing the days and shook on it, so the plan probably felt fair and not something forced by an elder sibling.

grounding: Siblings agree that alternate days belong to each, thinking about fairness and noting some days suit one child's homework better.

subtype: Approach: writing the schedule on a shared chart [Action]
passage:
Sunday. Sarita took a sheet of paper and a ruler and drew a table: seven days across, two names down the side, blue for Madhav and orange for herself. Under each day she coloured the boxes for the tablet: half an hour each. She stuck it on the fridge with a magnet.

Tuesday. Madhav opened the fridge, looked at the boxes and said, "It's blue today, right?" "Yes," said Sarita. No argument.

Next Sunday. They coloured the new week together. "Better than shouting," said Madhav. Sarita nodded.

qa.q: Which colour stands for Madhav on the chart?
qa.a: Blue stands for Madhav.

qa.q: How did Sarita probably feel when Madhav checked the chart without arguing?
qa.a: Sarita was probably pleased and relieved, since the chart settled the question with 'Yes' and no argument.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the children use if the chart is forgotten, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a parent to check the chart or use a kitchen timer for each turn. A neutral helper stops small disagreements from growing.

qa.q: How does the chart feel to Madhav?
qa.a: Madhav checked it calmly and said it was better than shouting, so Madhav finds it fair and easy to follow.

grounding: A girl draws a weekly table with names and colours on the fridge, so the children can check the written plan instead of arguing from memory.

subtype: Approach: negotiating by swapping what each values [Thinking]
passage: In the front room of their house in the small town, Mohit had a plan for Saturday morning: the family computer, a new game and nobody bothering him. But his sister Waheeda wanted the same computer on Sunday for her science project. "I need it more," said Mohit. "So do I," said Waheeda. Then Mohit thought. "What matters to me is Saturday morning, when my friends are online. What matters to you is a long stretch to finish the project." "Sunday afternoon," said Waheeda. "Then we swap: Saturday morning for me, Sunday for you." They shook hands, and neither of them lost.

qa.q: What did Waheeda want the computer for?
qa.a: Waheeda wanted the computer for her science project.

qa.q: What did Mohit realise about what mattered to each of them?
qa.a: Mohit realised that Saturday morning mattered to him because of his friends, while Waheeda needed a long stretch on Sunday for the project.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Mohit and Waheeda use, and why?
qa.a: They could split the time on one day into fixed halves with a timer. Either way, each gets some of what matters most to them.

qa.q: How might Waheeda see the swap?
qa.a: Waheeda agreed to Sunday afternoon and shook hands, so Waheeda probably feels the swap gave what the project needed and that Mohit listened.

grounding: A boy wants the computer on Saturday morning for a game and his sister wants it on Sunday for a project, so they swap to give each the time that matters.

subtype: Approach: telling the younger one to wait forever [Pitfall]
passage: In the small flat in Osaka, Hiroshi held the game controller and did not look up. "Big brother, can I have a turn?" Esther asked. "Later," said Hiroshi. An hour passed. "Now?" "Later." Another hour. Esther sat with her chin on the sofa arm, watching the screen without playing. At six she stood up, walked to the kitchen and said quietly to her mother, "Hiroshi says later, but it never comes." Mama put down the knife. She had to stop dinner, come into the living room, and take the controller herself to sort out whose turn it was. Hiroshi complained. Esther said nothing, but she looked tired.

qa.q: Where did Esther go at six o'clock?
qa.a: Esther went to the kitchen to talk to her mother.

qa.q: What was Esther feeling as she sat watching without playing?
qa.a: Esther felt ignored and disappointed, since 'later' never came and she was left watching. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Hiroshi use, and why?
qa.a: Hiroshi could say when the turn starts, such as after this level, and keep the promise. A clear time lets Esther trust that the wait will end.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Mama?
qa.a: Mama had to stop cooking to settle a turn between two children, so Mama probably feels interrupted and wishes they had agreed on it alone.

grounding: An elder brother tells his little sister she can have a turn later but later never comes, so she feels ignored and their mother has to step in.

subtype: Approach: changing the plan when exams come [Revision]
passage:
Afreen: Minakshi, you got the tablet for two days in a row this week and I'm not complaining. But I saw your face last night.
Minakshi: I wasn't going to say anything. I know you have exams.
Afreen: That's the thing. The plan doesn't fit any more. On my exam days, you should get more time.
Minakshi: Really?
Afreen: For two weeks, until my papers are done. You have it first every evening.
Minakshi: And then?
Afreen: Then it balances back, or we make a new plan. Deal?
Minakshi: Deal. Thanks, Afreen di.

qa.q: For how long did Afreen say Minakshi would get extra time?
qa.a: Afreen said for two weeks, until the papers are done.

qa.q: What did Afreen notice about Minakshi's face, and what might Minakshi have been feeling?
qa.a: Afreen noticed Minakshi's face the night before, which suggests Minakshi felt disappointed or left out, though Minakshi tried not to say so.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Afreen and Minakshi use, and why?
qa.a: They could set a fixed short time for Afreen to use the tablet after study, or ask a parent to help. Any plan should fit both children's needs.

qa.q: How does the new plan look to Minakshi?
qa.a: Minakshi asked 'Really?' and thanked Afreen, so Minakshi seems surprised and relieved that Afreen noticed and offered a fix.

grounding: When the older sibling has exams, the children notice the schedule is unfair, talk, and agree the younger gets more time for two weeks.

subtype: Approach: finding a game they can play together [Thinking]
passage: It had been raining all day, and there was only one game console in the house. Salma and her brother Harsha both wanted the controller. "My turn!" "No, mine!" They were about to start again when Salma stopped and looked at the shelf. "We keep asking whose turn it is," she said. "That's the wrong question. What could the two of us play together?" Harsha blinked. "There's the racing game that has two controllers." They plugged in the second one, sat side by side, and spent the afternoon racing each other around the track, laughing about who crashed into the barrier the most.

qa.q: What kind of game did Harsha and Salma choose?
qa.a: They chose the racing game with two controllers.

qa.q: What did Salma think about the fight over turns?
qa.a: Salma thought whose turn it was was the wrong question and that it was better to ask what they could both do, which shows a shift in thinking.

qa.q: What alternative approach could they use if the two-player game becomes boring, and why?
qa.a: They could use a timer to share turns or choose a board game. Either gives a fair option without a fight.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Salma's new question?
qa.a: Harsha blinked, then found the racing game right away, so Harsha probably felt surprised and happy to swap arguing for playing together.

grounding: Instead of fighting over the game, two siblings choose a two-player game, reframing the problem from whose turn to what they can do together.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to decide when stuck [Revision]
passage:
Tuesday. Siblings Afreen and Gopika tried to fix the schedule three times. Each time it ended with shouting and crossed arms.

Wednesday. "We can't do this by ourselves," said Gopika. "Let's ask Amma." Amma listened while each of them spoke, without interrupting, then wrote a timetable on the back of an envelope and read it out. "Do you both agree to keep to it?" Two slow nods.

Sunday. The envelope was stuck to the door. "It's your turn," said Gopika, and Afreen picked up the remote without a word of complaint.

qa.q: Where was the envelope with the timetable put?
qa.a: The envelope was stuck to the door.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel about trying alone, and what led to asking Amma?
qa.a: Gopika felt that the tries had failed and that they could not do it alone, so Gopika suggested asking Amma.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Afreen and Gopika try before asking Amma next time, and why?
qa.a: They could take a break to cool down and then write down what each needs. Calmer talk can lead to a fair plan without a referee.

qa.q: How might Amma see the timetable request?
qa.a: Amma listened to both without interrupting and asked for agreement, so Amma probably feels the children trust her and want a fair rule.

grounding: After several failed talks, the siblings agree to ask their mother to make the timetable, and Amma hears both and sets a rule they follow.
